newsitem.title: MACAU: Cyanide containers remain in south China river.
newsitem.headline: Cyanide containers remain in south China river.

text.p: Several containers of toxic cyanide remained submerged in a southern China tributary of the Pearl River on Wednesday despite clean-up efforts, Chinese sources in Macau said.

Authorities in southern China earlier issued a poison alert after reports that a truck carrying potassium cyanide fell into a river in Guangxi province, Macau government and Chinese local authorities said.
The river flows into the South China Sea west of Macau.

Reports on the number of cylinders on the truck ranged from 200 to 400, but most sources in the Portuguese-run enclave agreed that all but two or three had been recovered from the river by Wednesday afternoon.
There were also conflicting reports on whether any of the toxic chemical had leaked into the water. Chinese sources said all of the recovered cylinders were intact, but this could not be confirmed.
Chinese sources said any chemical released in the accident, which took place about 200 km (125 miles) northwest of Macau, would take about three days to reach the waters around the enclave.
Officials in Macau and the Chinese city of Zhuhai just across the border said they were monitoring the situation closely. Macau gets most of its tap water from Zhuhai.
Potassium cyanide -- used in the electroplating industry and in the extraction of gold and silver -- dissolves in water and is toxic, a chemist at a Hong Kong government laboratory said.
"It's a very toxic chemical," senior chemist S.K. Choi told Reuters, but added that the enormous flow rate of the Pearl River would "have a very large dilution effect".
Choi said the laboratory was expecting samples of river water to arrive for analysis.
"It's just a precautionary measure -- not that we expect there will be any acute toxicity," Choi said.
A Macau water company spokesman said the enclave's water supply was "absolutely safe" and that reserves were sufficient to last 45 days.
Supermarkets in central Macau reported a 20 percent rise in sales of bottled water since the potential spill was reported on Tuesday evening.
A spokesman at the Zhuhai city hall said public departments, hotels and the population of about 430,000 had been advised not to use untreated water from the West River and its tributaries.

"The Chinese authorities appear to take the possible threat very seriously, even though it is not known whether any of the containers actually leaked any (potassium cyanide)," a resident of Zhongshan city, about 50 km (30 miles) north of Macau, told Reuters.
